Part 4 of Block Diffusion RooflinesPrevious: 3 · Throughput calculatorNext: 5 · Empirical rooflines

We now present a set of exercises to get a better grasp and intuition on those rooflines. Here, the idea is to perform some napkin math so the answers to those exercises is more about getting the formula and the leading order (or trend) right than it is about precise numerics.

Numbers and rules

Exercise 1: reading the roofline

Figure 15 · interactive

Roofline graph.

In Questions 1 and 2, we focus on the case of short context, i.e., a 1k context. Hence, the network can be approximated by its linear layers.

  1. Heights and throughput. What is the relationship between the heights of the two points and the throughput gain \(\Gamma\)?

    Solution

    First, let us describe what the roofline graph is plotting. On the roofline graph, the \(y\)-axis is describing how much FLOPs are consumed per second. We recall that one forward pass corresponds to \(F\) FLOPs. The time for one forward pass is the maximum between the time it takes to perform calculations and the time it takes to move bytes. Hence, we have

    \[ T = \max\left( \frac{F}{\pi}, \frac{Q}{\beta}\right), \]

    Hence, the attainable FLOP/s \(R\), i.e., the height of a point on the roofline graph, is given by

    \[ R = F/T = \pi \min\left( 1, \frac{F \beta}{Q \pi}\right) = \pi \min\left( 1, \frac{I}{I^\star}\right). \]

    Hence, on a logarithmic scale we have

    \[ \log_{10}(R) = \log_{10}(\pi) + \min\left( 0, \log_{10}(I) - \log_{10}(I^\star) \right). \]

    Denote \(\class{mj-ar}{R^{\mathrm{AR}}} = \pi \min \left( 1, \frac{\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}{I^{\star}}\right)\) and \(\class{mj-td}{R^{\mathrm{TD}}} = \pi \min \left( 1, \frac{\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}}}{I^{\star}}\right)\). Then the ratio of the heights is given by

    \[ \frac{\class{mj-td}{R^{\mathrm{TD}}}}{\class{mj-ar}{R^{\mathrm{AR}}}} = \frac{\min(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}}, I^\star)}{\min(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}},I^\star)} . \]

    Now, we recall from Proposition 1 that, with \(\omega = Sr + 1\), \(S\) the number of denoising passes and \(r\) the cost of a denoising pass relative to a commit pass, we have that

    \[ \Gamma = \frac{1}{\omega}\cdot\frac{\min(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}},I^\star)}{\min(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}},I^\star)}. \]

    Therefore, we get

    \[ \Gamma = \frac{1}{\omega}\cdot\frac{\class{mj-td}{R^{\mathrm{TD}}}}{\class{mj-ar}{R^{\mathrm{AR}}}}. \]

    This means that the throughput gain is proportional to the ratio of the heights on the roofline, with constant \(1/\omega\).

  2. The best batch. Find where on the graph \(\Gamma\) is largest, and estimate \(\Gamma\) there.

    Solution

    AR is memory-bound here, since its intensity is about 2, far below \(I^\star = 206\). Hence, according to Corollary 1, we have that

    \[ \Gamma = \min\left(\frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi}, \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}\right) . \]

    Now, we have \(\frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi} \leq \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}\) if and only if \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} \leq I^\star\), since \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} = \frac{b \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}{\Pi}\). Hence, while TD is on the slope of the roofline graph, we have \(\Gamma = \frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi}\).

    Since the network can be approximated by its linear layers, we have that \(\Pi \approx \Pi_{\mathrm{lin}} = \frac{\class{mj-td}{W^{\mathrm{TD}}}(B)}{\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(B)}\), where we recall that \(W^X\) is the number of weights, in parameters, that the method \(X\) reads. In particular, with a canvas size \(256\), we have that \(\class{mj-td}{W^{\mathrm{TD}}}(B) \approx W_{\mathrm{tot}}\), even at \(B=1\), since all the experts are touched. Since \(\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(B)\) increases with \(B\), \(\Pi\) is non-increasing in \(B\), and Corollary 1 (2) applies: \(\Gamma\) is largest at the batch \(\class{mj-td}{B^{\mathrm{TD}}_\star}\) at which TD reaches the ridge.

    Indeed, while TD is memory-bound, \(\Gamma = \frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi}\) increases with \(B\). Once TD becomes compute-bound, i.e., \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} \geq I^\star\), it stays compute-bound, since \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}}\) is non-decreasing in \(B\) (Lemma 1). Since \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}\) is also non-decreasing in \(B\) (Lemma 1), \(\Gamma = \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}\) then decreases. Hence, the optimal point is reached when TD just becomes compute-bound, i.e., just at the beginning of the flat roofline for TD.

    On the graph this happens for \(\class{mj-td}{B^{\mathrm{TD}}_\star} \approx 6\), and the height ratio is then \(\approx 100\). Remembering the previous formula, we have then \(\Gamma \approx 100 / 15 \approx 6.5\), where we recall that \(\omega=15\).

  3. Large context. What changes at large context?

    Solution

    At large context, the KV cache carries most of the bytes and most of the FLOPs of both passes. Hence, according to Corollary 3, we have that

    \[ \Gamma = \min\left(\frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi_{\mathrm{attn}}}, \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}_{\mathrm{attn}}}}\right). \]

    A cache belongs to one sequence, so its bytes and FLOPs per sequence do not depend on the batch. Hence, at large context, the two points, and \(\Gamma\), no longer move with the batch.

    Now, on a global layer, a TD pass reads the same cache as an AR step and performs \(b\) times its FLOPs. Hence, we have that

    \[ \Pi_{\mathrm{attn}} = 1, \qquad \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \to I_{\mathrm{attn}} = 8, \qquad \class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} \to b\,I_{\mathrm{attn}} = 2{,}048. \]

    In particular, AR stays on the slope and TD on the roof, and the height ratio tends to \(I^\star/I_{\mathrm{attn}} \approx 206/8 \approx 26\). Therefore, we get

    \[ \Gamma \to \frac{I^\star}{\omega\, I_{\mathrm{attn}}} \approx \frac{26}{15} \approx 2. \]

Exercise 2: the gain along the batch

Figure 16

  1. Batch 1. Shrinking the canvas from 256 to 32 divides TPF by 8. Predict whether it also divides the penalty \(\Pi\) by 8, then give \(\Gamma\) at batch 1.

    Solution

    Let's have a look at the penalty. We are working at short context so the penalty is simply the ratio of the weights. We have that \(\Pi(1) = \frac{\class{mj-ar}{W_{AR}}(b)}{\class{mj-ar}{W_{AR}}(1)}\). Hence, ignoring the non-expert weights we have that

    \[ \Pi(1) \approx \frac{E}{k} \cdot \left[1 - \left(1-\frac{k}{E}\right)^b \right] . \]

    When \(b=32\), we have that

    \[\left(1-\frac{k}{E}\right)^b \approx 2^{-\frac{kb}{E \log(2)}} \approx 2^{-1.5 \cdot 2} \approx 1/8 .\]

    Hence, we have a reasonable approximation with \(\Pi(1) \approx \frac{E}{k} \approx 8\) no matter if \(b=256\) or if \(b=32\). The penalty is not divided by \(8\) in that scenario.

    Now, let us compute the throughput gain at \(B=1\). Since AR is memory bound, we have using Corollary 1, \[ \Gamma = \min\left(\frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi}, \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}\right) . \] Since at \(B=1\) we also have that TD is memory bound, we have that \[\Gamma = \frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi} .\] Hence, we get that \(\Gamma \approx \frac{32}{16 \cdot 8} \approx 0.25 \). Contrary to the setting where \(b=256\), due to the linear penalty, in this case, AR has a throughput advantage at small batch size.

  2. TD starts winning. From which batch does TD win?

    Solution

    While TD is memory bound, we have that the throughput gain is given by \(\Gamma = \frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi}\). We recall that \(\Pi(1) \approx 8\) hence, in order to find the batch at which TD wins we need to solve for \(B\) the following equation

    \[ \Pi(B) = \mathrm{TPF} \approx 2 .\]

    We recall that

    \[\Pi(B) \approx \frac{1 - \left( 1 - \frac{k}{E}\right)^{bB}}{1 - \left( 1 - \frac{k}{E}\right)^{B}} .\]

    Since at \(B=1\) already have shown that \(\left( 1 - \frac{k}{E}\right)^{bB}\approx 1/8\) we can approximate,

    \[\Pi(B) \approx \frac{1}{1 - \left( 1 - \frac{k}{E}\right)^{B}} .\]

    Hence, we need to solve for

    \[ \left( 1 - \frac{k}{E} \right)^{B} \approx 1/2 . \]

    Now, we have the approximation

    \[\left( 1 - \frac{k}{E}\right)^{B} \approx 2^{\frac{kB}{E\log(2)}} \approx 2^{\frac{1.5 \cdot kB}{E}} .\]

    Hence, we get that

    \[ 1.5 \cdot k B \approx E . \]

    Hence, we have \(B \approx 16 / 1.5 \approx 11\). In reality, we have that \(B\) is slightly lower with \(B \approx 8\). The main reason for this approximation is because we have neglected the non-expert weights.

  3. The best batch. At batch size is the gain maximal?

    Solution

    We recall from Exercise 1 that, when the penalty is non-increasing in the batch, \(\Gamma\) is largest at the batch \(\class{mj-td}{B^{\mathrm{TD}}_\star}\) at which TD reaches the ridge (Corollary 1 (2)). At short context, the network can be approximated by its linear layers. Hence, the intensity of a TD pass is

    \[ \class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} \approx \frac{2bBN_{\mathrm{act}}}{2\class{mj-td}{W^{\mathrm{TD}}}(B)} = \frac{bBN_{\mathrm{act}}}{\class{mj-td}{W^{\mathrm{TD}}}(B)}. \]

    From batch 2 on, a TD pass touches all the experts, i.e., \(\class{mj-td}{W^{\mathrm{TD}}}(B) \approx W_{\mathrm{tot}}\). Hence, we have that

    \[ \class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} \approx \frac{32 \cdot 3.1}{24.5}\, B \approx 4B. \]

    Therefore, TD reaches the ridge when \(4B \approx 206\), i.e., at

    \[ \class{mj-td}{B^{\mathrm{TD}}_\star} \approx 51. \]

    This is eight times the best batch of Exercise 1, since \(\class{mj-td}{B^{\mathrm{TD}}_\star} \propto 1/b\) (Corollary 2). Now, at this batch, the fraction of the experts that AR leaves untouched is

    \[ \left(1 - \frac{k}{E}\right)^{B} \approx 2^{-\frac{1.5\, kB}{E}} \approx 2^{-\frac{1.5 \cdot 51}{16}} \approx 2^{-5} \approx 3\%. \]

    Hence, AR also reads nearly all the weights, \(\Pi \approx 1\), and we get that

    \[ \Gamma \approx \mathrm{TPF} = \frac{32}{15} \approx 2.1. \]

    The best gain is therefore about 3 times smaller than in Exercise 1, not 8 times. Indeed, at \(b = 256\), the best batch is 6, and there AR reads \(1.7 + 22.8 \cdot (1 - (15/16)^6) \approx 9\)B parameters, so that the penalty is still

    \[ \Pi \approx \frac{W_{\mathrm{tot}}}{\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(6)} \approx \frac{24.5}{9} \approx 2.7. \]

    On the other hand, a short canvas reaches the ridge only at a batch at which AR touches nearly every expert, where the penalty vanishes.

    At a 1k context, a sequence also reads 0.2 GB of window cache at intensity 2 and 0.02 GB of global cache at intensity 8. Hence, a position costs \(6.2 + 0.4 + 0.16 \approx 6.8\) GFLOPs, and a TD pass costs, per sequence,

    \[ \class{mj-td}{F^{\mathrm{TD}}} \approx 32 \cdot 6.8 \approx 216 \text{ GFLOPs}, \qquad \class{mj-td}{Q^{\mathrm{TD}}} \approx \frac{49}{B} + 0.22 \text{ GB}. \]

    Setting \(\class{mj-td}{F^{\mathrm{TD}}}/\class{mj-td}{Q^{\mathrm{TD}}} = 206\) moves the ridge to about batch 60. On the map, the darkest orange lies below the solid line labelled \"TD compute-bound above\", and the peak is lower, about 1.8, because of the vocabulary matrix (Exercise 4).

  4. TD loses again. At which batch does AR catch up? Predict whether this batch depends on \(b\).

    Solution

    Beyond \(\class{mj-td}{B^{\mathrm{TD}}_\star}\), TD is compute-bound. Hence, according to Corollary 1, we have that

    \[ \Gamma = \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}. \]

    Therefore, \(\Gamma = 1\) when

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} = \frac{I^\star}{\omega} \approx \frac{206}{15} \approx 14. \]

    In particular, \(b\) does not appear: parity is at the same batch for every canvas long enough to reach the ridge before it.

    Without the cache, AR reads all the weights at these batches, and its intensity is

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx \frac{2BN_{\mathrm{act}}}{2W_{\mathrm{tot}}} \approx \frac{3.1}{24.5}\, B \approx \frac{B}{8}. \]

    Hence, parity would be at batch \(8 \cdot 14 \approx 110\) (Corollary 2). Now, at a 1k context, a sequence also reads 0.2 GB of window cache at intensity 2 and 0.02 GB of global cache at intensity 8. Hence, an AR step costs, per sequence,

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{F^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx 6.2 + 0.4 + 0.16 \approx 6.8 \text{ GFLOPs}, \qquad \class{mj-ar}{Q^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx \frac{49}{B} + 0.22 \text{ GB}. \]

    Setting \(\class{mj-ar}{F^{\mathrm{AR}}}/\class{mj-ar}{Q^{\mathrm{AR}}} = 14\), we get that

    \[ \frac{49}{B} + 0.22 \approx \frac{6.8}{14} \approx 0.49 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad B \approx 180. \]

    The window cache has intensity 2, below AR's linear intensity at these batches. Hence, it lowers AR's average intensity (Proposition 2) and delays parity. On the map, the upper branch of the thick dashed line sits near batch 110 rather than 180, because of the vocabulary matrix (Exercise 4); its agreement with the estimate without the cache is a coincidence.

Exercise 3: a dense model

We take a dense model, Llama 3.1 8B, on the H200, and pair it with a TD twin that has no self-conditioning. A dense model has no expert penalty, \(\Pi_{\mathrm{lin}} = 1\), and in BF16 its linear intensity is the batch: \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}_{\mathrm{lin}}}(B) = 2BN_{\mathrm{act}}/(2N_{\mathrm{act}}) = B\).

Figure 17

For a dense model, the roofline bound at context 1k is about 13 at batch 1 and falls like 1/B, to parity at batch 15.

  1. No penalty. With \(\Pi = 1\), a colleague expects \(\Gamma = \mathrm{TPF} \approx 17\) at batch 1 and short context. Find the flaw, give \(\Gamma\), and give the parity batch.

    Solution

    The colleague uses \(\Gamma = \mathrm{TPF}/\Pi\). We recall from Exercise 1 that this holds only while TD is memory-bound. With a dense model, \(\Pi = 1\), so that \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} = b\,\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}\). At batch 1 and short context, \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}_{\mathrm{lin}}}(1) = 1\). Hence, we have that

    \[ \class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} \approx 256 \gt I^\star = 206. \]

    Therefore, TD is already compute-bound at batch 1, and according to Corollary 1 we have that

    \[ \Gamma = \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}} \approx \frac{206}{15} \approx 14. \]

    This is the largest batch-1 gain of these exercises. Since \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}}\) is non-decreasing in \(B\) (Lemma 1), TD stays compute-bound, and \(\Gamma = I^\star/(\omega B)\) decreases with the batch. Hence, the best batch is batch 1 (Corollary 1 (2a)), and parity is at

    \[ B = \frac{I^\star}{\omega} \approx 14. \]

    Compared with Exercise 2, there is no losing phase: TD wins from batch 1, and its best batch is batch 1. On the map, the bottom row is dark orange, and the thick dashed line \(\Gamma = 1\) lies near batch 14.

  2. The cache and the ridge. At a 1k context, can any batch make AR compute-bound?

    Solution

    The weights are shared by the batch, so their bytes per sequence vanish as \(B \to \infty\). On the other hand, the cache belongs to one sequence and stays. At 1k tokens, a sequence reads \(1\text{k} \cdot 131\,\text{kB} \approx 0.13\) GB of cache, which carries \(4 \cdot 0.13 \approx 0.5\) GFLOPs. Hence, an AR step costs, per sequence,

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{F^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx 2N_{\mathrm{act}} + 0.5 \approx 14.5 \text{ GFLOPs}, \qquad \class{mj-ar}{Q^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx \frac{14}{B} + 0.13 \text{ GB}. \]

    Hence, as \(B \to \infty\), we have that

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \to \frac{14.5}{0.13} \approx 110 \lt I^\star = 206. \]

    Therefore, no batch makes AR compute-bound at this context (Proposition 9). Since TD is compute-bound (Question 1), \(\Gamma = I^\star/(\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}})\) keeps falling with the batch towards

    \[ \Gamma \to \frac{206}{15 \cdot 110} \approx 0.12, \]

    which is above the \(1/\omega \approx 0.07\) that a compute-bound AR would give (Corollary 1 (1)). For instance, at batch 256, a sequence reads \(14/256 \approx 0.055\) GB of weights and 0.13 GB of cache for 14.5 GFLOPs. Hence, we get that

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx \frac{14.5}{0.185} \approx 78, \qquad \Gamma \approx \frac{206}{15 \cdot 78} \approx 0.18. \]

    Finally, for a cache of \(Q_c\) bytes, AR can reach the ridge only if

    \[ \frac{14 \text{ GFLOPs}}{Q_c} + 4 \gt 206 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Q_c \lt 70 \text{ MB}, \]

    that is, a context of about 530 tokens. On the map, the 1k column stays blue above batch 15.

Exercise 4: a low ridge and the vocabulary

We go back to DiffusionGemma, on an H20, whose ridge point is about a fifth of the H200's (Table 3).

Figure 18

On an H20, whose ridge point is 37, the roofline bound puts TD ahead of AR only up to batch 4 at short context.

  1. What Proposition 1 leaves out. Proposition 1 ignores the vocabulary matrix, which DiffusionGemma's TD applies as the head of every denoising pass and, for self-conditioning, as a soft embedding in all but the first (Part 1, What the formulas leave out). At which batches does this omission overstate \(\Gamma\), on the H20 and on the H200, and by how much? What does it do to parity on the H20?

    Solution

    Applying the vocabulary matrix to one position costs \(2Vd \approx 1.5\) GFLOPs, i.e., 24% of the \(2N_{\mathrm{act}} \approx 6.2\) GFLOPs of the rest of the network. A TD position goes through \(\omega = 15\) passes, but it meets the matrix \(2S - 1 = 27\) times: as the head of the 14 denoising passes, and as the soft embedding of self-conditioning in 13 of them. Hence, once TD is compute-bound, its FLOPs, and hence its time, grow by a factor

    \[ 1 + \frac{27 \cdot 0.24}{15} \approx 1.43. \]

    Now, AR is memory-bound, and the matrix adds 0.74B parameters to the \(\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(B)\) its step reads. Hence, its time grows by a factor \(1 + 0.74/\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(B)\), with \(\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}\) in billions. Therefore, where TD is compute-bound, the omission overstates \(\Gamma\) by

    \[ \frac{1.43}{1 + 0.74/\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(B)}, \]

    which is about 1.3 at a few sequences, and 1.4 once AR reads all 24.5B parameters. On the H20, this holds from a few sequences on, since TD's batch-1 intensity, about 32, is already near the ridge, 37, and the matrix's FLOPs push it over. On the H200, it holds only above \(\class{mj-td}{B^{\mathrm{TD}}_\star} \approx 6\), and it moves the parity of Exercise 2 from about 180 to about 110. Below that batch, the matrix's bytes raise \(\Gamma\) slightly, since they weigh more in AR's bytes than in TD's.

    Let us now find parity on the H20. Without the matrix, parity is at

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}_{\mathrm{lin}}}(B) = \frac{I^\star}{\omega} \approx \frac{37}{15} \approx 2.5. \]

    At batch 10, AR leaves \((15/16)^{10} \approx 2^{-0.9} \approx 1/2\) of the experts untouched. Hence, it touches 64 experts per layer, reads \(1.7 + 30 \cdot 64 \cdot 6\text{M} \approx 13\)B parameters, and

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}_{\mathrm{lin}}}(10) \approx \frac{10 \cdot 3.1}{13} \approx 2.4. \]

    Hence, parity is near batch 10. With the matrix, \(\Gamma\) is divided by about 1.3, so parity needs

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}_{\mathrm{lin}}}(B) \approx \frac{2.5}{1.3} \approx 1.9. \]

    At batch 5, AR leaves \(2^{-0.5} \approx 0.7\) of the experts untouched. Hence, it touches 38 experts per layer, reads \(1.7 + 30 \cdot 38 \cdot 6\text{M} \approx 8.5\)B parameters, and

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}_{\mathrm{lin}}}(5) \approx \frac{5 \cdot 3.1}{8.5} \approx 1.8. \]

    Therefore, parity moves to about batch 5. In particular, a low ridge puts TD's whole winning range in the compute-bound regime, where every FLOP that Proposition 1 omits costs gain. On the map, which counts the matrix, the thick dashed line \(\Gamma = 1\) crosses the 1k column near batch 5.

Exercise 5: sparse attention

We go back to the H200 and replace DiffusionGemma's five global layers with the sparse layers of Remark 1 (Table 3), as in Figure 11.

  1. The limit. As the context grows, does TD win with \(S = 14\)? Up to which \(S\) does it win? Predict, then check the case \(S = 14\) against the shading of Figure 11, which is drawn for \(S = 14\).

    Solution

    As the context grows, the index scan carries most of the bytes and most of the FLOPs of both passes. Hence, according to Corollary 3 (2), we have that \(\Pi_{\mathrm{attn}} \to 1\), and

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \to I_{\mathrm{idx}} = 16, \qquad \class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} \to b\,I_{\mathrm{idx}} = 4{,}096. \]

    Since \(16 \lt 206 \lt 4{,}096\), TD's scan is compute-bound and AR's is memory-bound. Therefore, we get that

    \[ \Gamma \to \frac{I^\star}{\omega I_{\mathrm{idx}}} \approx \frac{206}{15 \cdot 16} \approx 0.86. \]

    Hence, AR wins. Indeed, AR runs its scan at \(16/206 \approx 8\%\) of the peak, and per committed token TD's 15 passes at the peak take longer than AR's step, since \(15 \gt 206/16 \approx 13\).

    Now, only \(\omega = Sr + 1\) depends on \(S\). Hence, \(\Gamma \propto 1/\omega\) at every batch and context, and TD wins in the limit when

    \[ \frac{206}{16\,\omega} \gt 1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \omega \lt 13 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S \le 11. \]

    Dense attention, at \(I_{\mathrm{attn}} = 8\), allows \(S \le 24\). Note that the limit assumes \(b\,I_{\mathrm{idx}} \gt I^\star\), i.e., a canvas of at least 13 positions. On a shorter canvas, both scans are memory-bound, and \(\Gamma \to \mathrm{TPF}\), which is below 1. In Figure 11, the shaded region \(\Gamma \lt 1\) reaches the right edge.

  2. Far from the limit. At 4M tokens, Figure 11 is shaded: Corollary 3 gives \(\Gamma \lt 1\). Does AR win at batch 1 with \(S = 14\)? Find the assumption that fails.

    Solution

    Corollary 3 assumes that attention carries most of the bytes. The index cache holds 640 B per token, so 4M tokens take 2.7 GB. On the other hand, at batch 1, AR reads 6.2 GB of weights and 0.2 GB of window cache. Hence, the assumption fails: the weights still carry about 0.7 of AR's bytes, and the index cache about 0.3. Therefore, according to Proposition 2, we have that

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx 0.7 \cdot 1 + 0.3 \cdot 16 \approx 5.5. \]

    Now, TD's 256 queries select \(U_{C,m}(b) \approx bm \approx 520\)k distinct tokens, since \(bm \ll C\), i.e., about 10.5 GB of global cache. Hence, TD reads about \(49 + 2.7 + 10.5 \approx 62\) GB against AR's 9 GB, and

    \[ \Pi \approx 7, \qquad \frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi} \approx \frac{17}{7} \approx 2.4, \qquad \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}} \approx \frac{206}{15 \cdot 5.5} \approx 2.5. \]

    Hence, according to Corollary 1, TD sits at the ridge, \(\Gamma \approx 2.4\), and TD wins.

    Parity at batch 1 needs \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx 14\), hence an index cache near 87% of AR's bytes, i.e., about 40 GB or 60M tokens. At 4M tokens, the global cache alone is about 85 GB, and the 141 GB of an H200 hold the weights and at most about 4.3M tokens of cache. Therefore, on one H200, the limit of Question 1 is out of reach.

Exercise 6: number formats

We keep DiffusionGemma on the H200 at a 1k context, and change the format of the weights, of the KV cache and of the matrix multiplications. A format of \(s\) bytes per value multiplies the intensity of what it stores by \(2/s\): \(s_w\) acts on \(I_{\mathrm{lin}}\) and \(s_{\mathrm{kv}}\) on \(I_{\mathrm{attn}} = 4g/(\kappa^c_\ell s_{\mathrm{kv}})\) (Definitions 1–3). The format of a multiplication sets the peak, and hence the ridge, at which its FLOPs run. The questions follow the roofline chapter of How to Scale Your Model, which compares int8 weights with BF16 and with int8 multiplications.

  1. A common speed-up. Weights and cache are in FP8, and every multiplication, attention included, runs at the FP8 peak. A colleague argues that this favours TD, which is compute-bound at its best batch and gains from the doubled peak. Find the flaw: does \(\Gamma\) change?

    Solution

    We recall from Proposition 1 that

    \[ \Gamma = \frac{1}{\omega}\cdot\frac{\min(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}},I^\star)}{\min(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}},I^\star)}. \]

    In FP8, every value takes 1 byte instead of 2, so every intensity doubles. Since every multiplication runs at the FP8 peak, the ridge \(I^\star\) doubles as well. Hence, both minima double, and \(\Gamma\) does not change, at any batch or context. In particular, a memory-bound AR step reads half the bytes, so it also runs twice as fast.

    A format changes \(\Gamma\) only when it speeds up the bytes and the FLOPs by different factors. For instance, take an FP8 cache read by BF16 attention. Then \(I_{\mathrm{attn}}\) doubles to 16, while the ridge of attention stays at 206. Hence, according to Corollary 3, the long-context limit becomes

    \[ \Gamma \to \frac{206}{15 \cdot 16} \approx 0.86, \]

    as with the index scan of Exercise 5.

  2. Fewer bytes than FLOPs. NVFP4 weights, once on the H200, which has no FP4 multiplication and converts them to BF16, and once on the B200, which multiplies them at its FP4 peak; the cache stays in BF16. Predict which setting acts like a lower BF16 ridge, then give each one's best gain.

    Solution

    Weights of \(s_w\) bytes multiply the linear intensities by \(2/s_w\), and multiplications that run \(\sigma\) times faster than BF16 multiply the ridge by \(\sigma\). We recall from Question 1 that \(\Gamma\) depends only on the intensities divided by the ridge. Hence, each setting acts like BF16 on an accelerator with ridge \(\rho I^\star\), where

    \[ \rho = \frac{\sigma}{2/s_w}. \]

    With \(s_w \approx 0.56\) (Table 3), we have \(2/s_w \approx 3.6\). We neglect the BF16 cache, which at 1k tokens is a sixth to a quarter of AR's bytes at these batches once the weights are in NVFP4, and which raises the gains below by about 15%. At \(b = 256\), we recall from Question 3 of Exercise 2 that, with all experts touched, \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} \approx 256 \cdot 3.1\, B/24.5 \approx 32B\).

    On the H200, \(\sigma = 1\). Hence, \(\rho = 1/3.6\), and the ridge is \(206/3.6 \approx 57\). Hence, the corner is at \(32B \approx 57\), i.e., near batch 2. There, AR touches 15 experts per layer and reads \(1.7 + 30 \cdot 15 \cdot 6\text{M} \approx 4.4\)B parameters. Therefore, we get that

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx \frac{2 \cdot 3.1}{4.4} \approx 1.4, \qquad \Gamma \approx \frac{57}{15 \cdot 1.4} \approx 2.7. \]

    On the B200, \(\sigma = 4\). Hence, \(\rho = 4/3.6 \approx 1.1\), and the ridge is \(1{,}125/3.6 \approx 310\). Hence, the corner is at \(32B \approx 310\), i.e., near batch 10. There, AR leaves \(2^{-0.94} \approx 0.52\) of the experts untouched, touches 61 per layer and reads \(1.7 + 30 \cdot 61 \cdot 6\text{M} \approx 12.7\)B parameters. Therefore, we get that

    \[ \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx \frac{10 \cdot 3.1}{12.7} \approx 2.4, \qquad \Gamma \approx \frac{310}{15 \cdot 2.4} \approx 9, \]

    against about 8 at the B200's BF16 ridge of 281.

    Hence, when the weight bytes shrink by more than the multiplications speed up, \(\rho \lt 1\), and the setting acts like a lower ridge, which lowers both the best batch and the best gain (Corollary 2). This is the case of NVFP4 on the H200, and of FP8 weights converted to BF16 on an A100, which has no FP8 rate: \(\rho = 1/2\), so the batch at which a multiplication becomes compute-bound halves, as in How to Scale Your Model. On the other hand, NVFP4 on the B200 has \(\rho \gt 1\) and acts like a higher ridge. Finally, at batch 1, every setting keeps both decoders on the slope, and \(\Gamma \approx 2.1\).
